Notes: A desert robe of lightweight fabric covering the entire body; typical colours brown, gold, black and white. A silken or cotton sash ties it at the waist. In deserts and other dry climates such garments help prevent evaporation, letting the wearer retain more moisture; assuming adequate water, a character wearing a desert robe is no more likely to suffer heat exhaustion on days of extreme heat than a normal person on a day of moderate temperature. Desert robes do NOT help in areas of high humidity. PRINTED FOOTNOTE: price is double to triple this amount unless bought in a desert setting.

A hollow reed about a foot long, strengthened with wax and treated with waterproofing oil. The user places the tube in his mouth, then submerges himself with the end protruding from the water. Enables the submerged user to breathe INDEFINITELY. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

A compact leather case containing several cakes of greasepaint (browns, greens, yellows and black), applicator brushes, a jar of paint removal cream, and a small mirror. Applied to areas of exposed flesh. A kit contains 12 uses. By itself camouflage paint gives NO particular advantage; used with a terrain suit it boosts the character's success chance by +1. The camouflage proficiency is required to apply it well -- those without the proficiency have HALF the usual chance of success. A character using camouflage paint AND a terrain suit gains a +2 bonus to his camouflage check.

A wooden frame for carrying supplies, wooden runners extending the length of the sled, a platform on which the passenger stands, and a lattice at the front to which the dog team is harnessed. About 6-11 dogs (or equivalent) can pull a sled 10 ft long and 3 ft wide, carrying up to 880 pounds INCLUDING the weight of the sled; fewer animals are required for smaller sleds. A typical 8-dog sled travels at movement rate 15 with a load of about 680 lbs including the sled. DMs should take into account that animals not bred or trained to pull a sled can create considerable trouble for the driver -- tangling traces, fighting with nearby animals -- and movement could be slower than expected.
Also called a perch glove. A heavy arm-length glove of thick leather upon which a falcon or hawk can perch.

Makes falcon training more efficient. A character using the falconry proficiency WITHOUT this equipment suffers a -2 penalty to training proficiency checks. One set is required for each falcon. Each set consists of jesses (leather bands with rings, attached to the falcon's legs), talon guards (metal coverings for the bird's claws to prevent it harming the owner during training), a creance (a slender leather leash attached to the jesses, held by the user or secured to the perch glove), and a hood (a leather covering fitting over the falcon's head that restricts vision, forcing the falcon to rely on hearing, touch and taste). Customized or richly appointed equipment, such as an embroidered hood or golden jesses, is also available, usually at double or triple the normal price.

A single-person boat, fast-moving and easy to manoeuvre. A lashed wooden frame about ten feet long and two feet wide, covered with canvas, sealskins or hides of similar water-dwelling animals, attached to the frame, allowed to tighten by drying, then coated with oil to make the craft water resistant. The passenger squeezes into the hole in the top and sits so his legs extend into the bow. To seal out water the opening has an apron, often made of whale intestines, which the kayaker laces around his waist. Propelled with a single long oar with a paddle on either end. Movement 200 ft/round (may be rounded down to 6).

A pungent liquid used to attract animals in the wild. Each scent lure attracts a SPECIFIC type of animal, usually woodland game such as deer, wolf or fox; individual animals of the species find the odour irresistible. Each bottle contains five applications. One application near a tree, rock or snare has a 15% chance of attracting an animal of the given species within 24 hours, presuming the animal passes within 100 yards of the application -- the DM determines whether an animal comes close enough. Extra applications do NOT increase the chance. The scent evaporates in 24 hours. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

Arctic or mountaineering goggles made from solid wood; the wearer peers through two narrow slits. These reduce or eliminate the effects of dazzling lights, such as fatigue from travelling under very bright sun -- across deserts, or flat plains on cloudless days. They also PREVENT SNOWBLINDNESS, where the eyes become swollen from exposure to bright sun reflecting off ice and snow; attack penalties for snowblindness vary from -1 to -4. They will NOT prevent blindness caused when a light spell is cast directly against the wearer's eyes. They also reduce the field of vision -- the wearer cannot see above or below without moving his head, which may increase chances of being surprised or attacked from a blind side, at the DM's option. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

Characters risk damage from sunburn in any terrain during seasons of bright sunlight, not only in deserts but also in the arctic, where the sun reflects off the ice and snow. If characters do not protect exposed flesh with scarves, mask or other covering, they risk suffering 1 point of damage from sunburn PER DAY. An application gives protection against sunburn for a full day. A jar contains 14 applications. Gives NO protection from magical or non-magical fire, and is ineffective against any source of damage other than the sun. Rare, found only in the best-stocked shops in large cities. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

A small leather pouch, about four inches on each side and an inch thick, strapped around the thigh, upper arm or anywhere else it can remain concealed. Contains a scrap of parchment and piece of graphite (for writing messages), a fish hook, a 25-foot length of fishing line on a spool, one gold piece (good for bribing guards), a small razor (for severing rope or inflicting 1 hit point of damage against captors), a wooden whistle (for signaling), a cloth pad (for making an emergency bandage), and a few pieces of sugar candy and dried fruit (for quick energy, or luring animals). Similar items may be substituted to customize individual kits. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

One of the simplest tents: a single sheet of fabric arranged around a pole to form a cone, with ropes attached to stakes surrounding the bottom pulled to stretch the fabric tight. Quick to construct and easy to transport, but bell tents do NOT provide much protection against strong winds. Suitable for one or two occupants.

Particularly useful in cold climates. Consists of six to eight ribs about five feet long, connected to each other by the tent covering. The covering is two layers of skin from a furry animal such as a bear or caribou, arranged fur-side out, creating a pocket of air for extra insulation. Opens like an umbrella to form a domed shape, or folds into a bundle. Suitable for one or two occupants.
Canvas pavilion tent

Combines elements of the bell and wedge tents. The frame is four vertical poles arranged in a square with horizontal poles attached between them; a longer pole rises from the centre of the square, and the fabric extends from the centre pole to form four slanting walls, secured with stakes. The sturdy pyramid tent RESISTS LIGHT TO MODERATE WINDS. Suitable for one or two occupants.
Canvas tent for 1-2 people

Also known as an A-frame tent or a wall tent. Built on a frame of two vertical poles with a horizontal pole secured between them; the fabric is laid across the horizontal pole, then stretched with ropes attached to stakes. Somewhat sturdier than the bell tent, although like that tent it provides only modest protection against severe weather. Suitable for one or two occupants.

NOT PRICED IN THE BOOK -- Chapter 7 describes the terrain suit but Table 57 gives it no cost or weight. Lightweight linen or silk; a long-sleeved shirt or blouse and long trousers dyed to help the wearer blend in. Styles: arctic (solid white), sand (mottled browns), woodland (greens and browns), urban (black). Must be precisely made and fitted to its wearer. Gives the same advantages as the camouflage proficiency when worn in the appropriate terrain, using a base Wisdom rating of 14; a character who also has the camouflage proficiency uses his own Wisdom (or 14, whichever is higher) with an additional +1 bonus. As a rule of thumb terrain suits should be slightly more common than elven chain mail. A Stalker receives one free at the start of his career.

A waterproof box containing flint and steel along with a small supply of wood shavings for kindling. Keeps the contents dry during a rainstorm or when submerged underwater. ONCE PER ROUND a character can attempt to start a fire using these materials: a roll of 1 or 2 on 1d8 is necessary in normal, dry conditions; a 1 on 1d8 is necessary if the area is damp. The DM may require more difficult rolls -- for instance a 1 on 1d12 in wet terrain -- or may rule that a fire cannot be started at all. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).

A finely-crafted metal trap that can be set up in a matter of minutes. An enclosing trap resembles a box and catches animals ALIVE: lured by edible bait or a shiny object, the animal enters the box and steps on a trigger which causes the front of the box to snap shut. A character using either type of trap adds a +1 bonus to his set snares proficiency checks. Small is the rabbit size.
As the small killing trap; large is the bear size. A character using either type of trap adds a +1 bonus to his set snares proficiency checks.
As the small killing trap; medium is the wolf size. A character using either type of trap adds a +1 bonus to his set snares proficiency checks.

A finely-crafted metal trap that can be set up in a matter of minutes. A killing trap has two metal jaws lined with sharp points; a small platform, which holds a lure, rests in between the jaws, and the slightest pressure on the platform causes the jaws to snap shut, killing the animal. A character using either type of trap adds a +1 bonus to his set snares proficiency checks. Small is the rabbit size.

Resembles a dog sled with inflated skins in place of runners, enabling the craft to float on the surface of the water. Long leather reins, treated with waterproofing oil, connect with the animals pulling it -- usually a team of eight seals or six dolphins. Carries no more than two passengers (about 480 pounds, including the sled) unless the animals pulling it are exceptionally fast and strong. Made to ride as much above the water as in it, it can achieve a top movement rate of 15 if pulled by strong steeds, but 9-12 is a more sustainable speed.

An oily paste rangers or thieves apply to their weapons or armor to make the metallic surfaces non-reflective and nearly invisible, modifying their base chance to hide in shadows by +5%. A coat lasts until the character engages in melee combat, at which point enough of the substance flakes away to negate any camouflaging advantage. The substance is FLAMMABLE: if lighted, a sword coated with the paste becomes the equivalent of a flametongue for 2-5 rounds, and will also inflict 1d4 points of heat damage upon the wielder unless he is magically protected. A vial contains 1 application. PRINTED FOOTNOTE: rare, and only available under-the-counter. Weight is inconsequential (a few ounces).
